title: Block-wise Codeword Embedding for Reliable Multi-bit Text Watermarking
claim: Prior schemes map every token to a segment so ECC accepts any codeword; ours embeds codewords in blocks and verifies by window-shifting.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right flow, nested rounded insets under arrows
description: Two horizontal rows show two watermarking pipelines. The top row, the prior scheme, starts with a colored Message m split into segments Seg0 to Seg3. It passes through a binary token-to-segment mapping matrix and then into a grid of pastel Token boxes colored by segment, and it ends in a reconstructed Message m bar. The bottom row, BREW, starts with a blue Message m bar. This feeds a Codeword Set C of colored rows with codeword length n. Next is a larger token grid where each row of tokens is colored by its codeword. A final rounded box lists the embedded codewords, with green circles for matches and a red X for a failed one. Insets underneath show the codeword-bit to G/R list mapping, with rule 0↔R and 1↔G, and Window-Shifting Detection, with left and right arrows over bit strings compared with 'vs'.
caption: Comparison of multi-bit watermarking frameworks. (Top) Prior schemes map every token to a segment, allowing ECC to "correct" accumulated noise into valid codewords, leading to high false positives. (Bottom) BREW employs distributed embedding and window-shifting with designated verification. This eliminates "any-codeword" acceptance, preserving payload capacity while strictly controlling false positives.
abstract: Recent multi-bit watermarking methods for large language models (LLMs) prioritize capacity over reliability, often conflating decoding with detection. Our analysis reveals that existing ECC-based extractors suffer from catastrophic false positive rates (FPR), and applying rejection thresholds merely collapses detection sensitivity (TPR) to random guessing. To resolve this structural limitation, we propose BREW (Block-wise Reliable Embedding for Watermarking), a framework shifting the paradigm to designated verification. BREW employs a two-stage mechanism: (i) blind message estimation via independent block voting, followed by (ii) window-shifting verification that rigorously validates the payload against local edits. Experiments demonstrate that BREW achieves a TPR of 0.965 with an FPR of 0.02 under 10% synonym substitution, demonstrating that the high-FPR issue is not an inherent trade-off of multi-bit watermarking, but a solvable structural flaw of prior decoding-centric designs. Our framework is model-agnostic and theoretically grounded, providing a scalable solution for reliable forensic deployment.
